title: The Redeemer Will Come to Zion
summary: God's arm is not too short to save; the people's sins have built a wall between them and him. The prophet describes a society where violence, lies, and injustice are everywhere, and the people join in a confession: they grope like the blind at noon, and truth has stumbled in the public square. Seeing that no one intervenes, the LORD himself puts on righteousness as armor and comes to repay his enemies and to redeem those in Jacob who turn from sin, promising that his Spirit and his words will never leave them.
story: Chapter 58 answered the people's complaint that God did not notice their fasting. Chapter 59 answers a deeper complaint, that God seems unable or unwilling to save. The answer echoes 50:2: his hand is not too short. The problem is sin. But the chapter does not stop at accusation. It moves to confession and then to God's own intervention, because no human is able to set things right. The Divine Warrior who arms himself here reappears in 63:1-6, and the promise of the Redeemer coming to Zion prepares for the dawn of glory in chapter 60.
historical: The chapter describes a community in moral collapse: bloodshed, perjury, legal injustice, and people who turn from evil becoming prey. Most scholars locate it in the postexilic period, when the hopes of the return had not materialized and Judah remained small, poor, and under Persian rule. Prophets of that period, such as Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, address similar disappointment and similar sins. On the traditional reading the same conditions fit Judah before the exile, which Isaiah and his contemporary Micah condemned (Micah 3). The communal confession in verses 9 to 15 has close parallels in prayers from the period after the exile, including Ezra 9, Nehemiah 9, and Daniel 9, in which leaders confess the sins of the whole people, including their own generation.
cultural:
The public square of verse 14 translates a word for a town's open plaza. Such squares often lay by the city gate, where elders sat to hear lawsuits and settle disputes (compare Ruth 4:1-2; Amos 5:15). When truth stumbles there, the whole system of justice fails, and ordinary people have nowhere to turn. The images of verses 5 and 6 come from nature: viper eggs, which produce death when hatched, and spider webs, which look like cloth but cannot be woven into clothing. Both describe schemes that are either deadly or useless.

The armor of verse 17 draws on the equipment of an ancient soldier: the breastplate that protected the chest, the helmet, and the cloak worn over it. Pictures of gods as warriors were common across the ancient Near East, and Israel also sang of the LORD as a warrior (Exodus 15:3). What stands out here is what he wears: righteousness, salvation, vengeance, and zeal, qualities rather than metal.
literary: The chapter moves through three voices. Verses 1 to 8 are the prophet's accusation, addressed first to “you” (verses 1 to 3) and then describing “they” (verses 4 to 8), with a dense catalog of body parts turned to evil: hands, fingers, lips, tongue, feet. Verses 9 to 15a switch to “we,” a communal lament and confession in which the people admit that the prophet's charges are true. Verses 15b to 21 are a narrative of God's action: he looks, sees no one, and acts himself. The chapter ends in prose with a covenant promise (verse 21), whose wording about Spirit and words in the mouth recalls 51:16 and anticipates 61:1.

outline.t: Not a short arm but a wall of sin
The people's confession: groping at noon, and the LORD sees
The LORD puts on righteousness as armor
The Redeemer comes to Zion: an enduring covenant

doctrines.note: “Your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God” (verse 2). Sin is not only a list of acts but a separation, and the chapter shows its social face: violence, deceit, and a justice system that no longer works.
The people's “we” confession (verses 9 to 15) is a model of repentance: specific, communal, and without excuse. The Redeemer comes “to those in Jacob who turn from transgression” (verse 20).
When God saw that there was no one to intercede, “His own arm brought salvation” (verse 16). Salvation here is God's initiative when human effort has failed completely.

The covenant of verse 21 promises that God's Spirit and his words will not depart from his people or their descendants. The Spirit is the guarantee that God's people will go on hearing and speaking his word.

words.note: Paga, to meet, strike, or intercede. In verse 16 God is amazed that no one intercedes, that is, no one steps into the gap on the people's behalf. The same verb describes the Servant in 53:12, who made intercession for the transgressors. The chapter's missing intercessor is the one chapter 53 described.

Gaal, to redeem, to act as a go'el, the kinsman-redeemer who bought back family land or a relative sold into slavery and avenged wrongs (Leviticus 25:25, 47-49). God calls himself Israel's go'el often in Isaiah. The Redeemer who comes to Zion (verse 20) acts as the nearest relative of a helpless people.

Mishpat, justice, the right ordering of relationships, especially through fair judgment. It appears five times in the chapter, always absent: there is no justice in their tracks, justice is far from us, justice is turned away. The chapter's repetition makes the absence felt.

christ: Paul draws on this chapter in two major places. In Romans 3:15-17 he quotes verses 7 and 8 as part of his case that all have sinned, Jew and Gentile alike. In Romans 11:26-27 he quotes verses 20 and 21, in the Greek form that says the deliverer will come from Zion and turn ungodliness away from Jacob, to argue that God's covenant with Israel still stands and will end in Israel's salvation. The divine armor of verse 17 becomes the believer's armor in Ephesians 6:14-17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8: the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation. The chapter's picture of God acting alone because no one could intercede is read by Christians as fulfilled in Christ, God's own arm, who is also the intercessor (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25).

hard.q: Is God's vengeance in verses 17 and 18 compatible with his love?
hard.a: The LORD puts on garments of vengeance and repays fury to his enemies. Some readers find this at odds with the God of compassion elsewhere in Isaiah. Several points help. First, vengeance in the Bible is not personal spite but the restoration of justice by the rightful judge; it belongs to God precisely so that people will not take it into their own hands (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19). Second, the context is a world where the innocent are prey and there is no justice; a God who never acted against oppressors would not be loving to their victims. Third, the same passage offers redemption to anyone who turns from transgression (verse 20), which means the line between enemies and redeemed is not ethnic but moral. Readers still differ on how to hold wrath and love together, but Scripture consistently holds both.

questions: Verse 14 pictures truth stumbling in the public square. Where do you see that today, and what part might you play in it?
The chapter moves from accusation to confession using “we.” Why does confessing sin as a community matter, not only as individuals?
God acts because there was no one to intercede. Who might need you to stand in the gap for them in prayer or in action?
